meta.title: shadcn/ui vs Mantine: Which to Choose in 2026?
meta.description: shadcn/ui vs Mantine comparison: styling, components, theming, maintenance, and architecture trade-offs for product teams.

verdict: Choose shadcn/ui if you want copy-in React components that you own and customize, are comfortable with Tailwind CSS, and prefer full control over markup and styling. Choose Mantine if you want a batteries-included component library with hooks, form utilities, and theming that works well without Tailwind. Both are actively maintained and production-ready; the right pick depends on how much ownership and styling freedom you need versus how much built-in functionality you want out of the box.

comparison.toolA: shadcn/ui is not a traditional dependency you install and import; its components are copied into your repository through a CLI or generated manually, so you own the source and can edit it freely. It relies on Radix UI primitives for behavior and Tailwind CSS for styling, which means the component code lives and evolves with your codebase. Updates are manual, so you decide when and how to adopt upstream changes.
comparison.toolB: Mantine is a conventional package-based component library published to npm and imported as dependencies (@mantine/core plus optional packages such as hooks and form). Its components ship as prebuilt modules with a consistent API, so version upgrades arrive through your package manager and documentation tracks each release. This makes it closer to a classic framework-level library than to a source-copying collection.

comparison.toolA: shadcn/ui covers the most commonly needed UI elements such as buttons, dialogs, menus, inputs, tables, and navigation patterns, built on accessible Radix primitives. Its scope is intentionally focused, so advanced or niche widgets often require composing primitives yourself or adding third-party libraries. The collection grows over time, but feature availability depends on the current version and what each component supports.
comparison.toolB: Mantine ships a broad catalog that spans layout, inputs, overlays, data display, charts, notifications, dates, and more, with additional packages for hooks and form state. Because it aims to be comprehensive, many project needs can be met without reaching for other libraries. Exact component availability and API details should be checked against the current major version, since Mantine has shipped breaking changes across releases.

comparison.toolA: shadcn/ui leans on Tailwind CSS utility classes plus CSS variables for themes, so styling changes usually mean editing classes or the copied component files directly. This gives fine-grained control and keeps styles colocated with markup, but it requires Tailwind familiarity and a willingness to maintain customized code. Global design changes often flow through CSS variables and Tailwind configuration.
comparison.toolB: Mantine uses its own styling system built around CSS modules, a theme object, and style props, with no Tailwind requirement. You can theme components centrally through MantineProvider and override styles via props or classes, which suits teams that prefer CSS-in-JS-adjacent patterns or plain CSS over utility classes. Customization is powerful but generally happens within Mantine's conventions rather than by rewriting component source.

comparison.category: Theming, design tokens, and dark mode
comparison.toolA: shadcn/ui handles theming largely through CSS variables defined in your global stylesheet, with dark mode typically wired to a class or attribute on the root element. Because the variables and component code are yours, you can implement custom color scales, radius, and typography tokens with full flexibility. Dark mode integration depends on how you configure Tailwind and your chosen theme strategy.
comparison.toolB: Mantine provides a first-class theme object with color schemes, built-in dark mode support, and utilities for color manipulation and CSS variables. Theme changes are centralized and typed, and the library documents how to extend or override defaults. This makes consistent theming across a large app straightforward, though deep structural changes may still require custom CSS.

comparison.toolA: shadcn/ui builds on Radix UI primitives, which handle focus management, keyboard interaction, and ARIA attributes for many complex widgets like dialogs, menus, and popovers. Accessibility is therefore strong for supported patterns, but it is not automatic for custom compositions you build yourself, and you remain responsible for testing. Behavior correctness depends on the current Radix and shadcn/ui versions.
comparison.toolB: Mantine components generally include keyboard support and ARIA attributes, and the project documents accessibility considerations for many components. Because components are prebuilt, baseline behavior is consistent, though complex customizations can still introduce gaps. As with any library, verify accessibility against your own requirements and current release notes rather than assuming full compliance.

comparison.toolA: shadcn/ui assumes comfort with React, Tailwind CSS, and the idea of owning component source, so newcomers to Tailwind may need time to adjust. Once set up, the mental model is simple: components are just files you can read and change. The CLI simplifies adding components, and documentation focuses on composition patterns rather than a large proprietary API.
comparison.toolB: Mantine offers a cohesive, documented API with typed props and examples, and it does not require Tailwind knowledge. The tradeoff is learning Mantine's theming, style props, and package structure, which can feel like adopting a framework. Teams already fluent in CSS and React often find the initial ramp-up moderate, and the extensive docs help.

comparison.toolA: shadcn/ui benefits from a large community and tight alignment with the Tailwind and Radix ecosystems, and because code is local, you are never blocked by upstream breaking changes. The flip side is that you own maintenance, including accessibility fixes and adaptations when dependencies change. Long-term fit is strongest for teams that want control and are prepared to maintain their component layer.
comparison.toolB: Mantine has an active maintainer team, regular releases, and a mature ecosystem including hooks, forms, and notifications packages. Upgrades are managed through package versions, which centralizes fixes but can require migration work when major versions change APIs. Long-term fit is strongest for teams that prefer a supported, integrated library over owning component internals.

comparison.category: Fit with design systems and large teams
comparison.toolA: shadcn/ui works well when you want to build a bespoke design system, since copied components can be refactored into your own abstractions and documented internally. It requires discipline around component ownership and upgrade strategy, especially across many contributors. Teams with strong frontend engineering capacity tend to get the most from this model.
comparison.toolB: Mantine suits teams that want consistent defaults and centralized theming without building a component layer from scratch. Its conventions can speed up delivery across large teams, though heavily bespoke visual requirements may need extra overrides. Governance is simpler because the library, not your repository, owns the component implementations.

faq.q: Is shadcn/ui a component library or a code generator?
faq.a: shadcn/ui is best understood as a collection of component source files distributed through a CLI rather than a traditional npm component library. You copy components into your project and own them, so you can edit markup and styles freely, but you also take on maintenance and upgrade decisions yourself.

No, Mantine has its own styling system based on CSS modules, a theme object, and style props, so Tailwind is not required. You can use Tailwind alongside Mantine if you want, but the library is designed to work without it, which matters if your team prefers plain CSS or a different styling approach.

faq.q: Which option is better for accessibility?
faq.a: Both projects take accessibility seriously: shadcn/ui builds on Radix UI primitives with focus and keyboard handling, while Mantine components generally include ARIA attributes and keyboard support. Neither guarantees compliance for your specific compositions, so test against WCAG requirements and your own user flows, and check current release notes for known issues.

faq.q: Can I use shadcn/ui and Mantine together in one project?
faq.a: Technically you can install both, but mixing two styling and theming systems tends to increase bundle size and create inconsistent design language. It is usually better to pick one as the primary UI layer and use the other only for narrowly scoped needs, if at all.

faq.q: How do upgrades and breaking changes compare?
faq.a: shadcn/ui updates are manual because components live in your repo, so you control when to adopt changes and can adapt them to your code. Mantine upgrades come through package versions, and major releases have historically included breaking API changes, so review migration guides before upgrading.

faq.q: Which is better for a large application with a custom design system?
faq.a: shadcn/ui is often a good fit when you want to build and own a bespoke design system, because component source can be refactored and documented internally. Mantine can also work at scale through centralized theming, but heavily customized visuals may require overrides within its conventions. Consider your team's capacity to maintain component code.

Yes, both support dark mode, though the mechanisms differ. shadcn/ui typically uses CSS variables plus a class or attribute strategy configured with Tailwind, while Mantine includes built-in color scheme handling and a theme object. Verify the current setup steps for your chosen versions and framework integration.

faq.q: Which should I choose for a small team shipping quickly?
faq.a: Mantine often reduces initial setup effort because it provides a broad, integrated component set and theming without Tailwind configuration. shadcn/ui can be fast too if your team already knows Tailwind and wants direct control over component code. Match the choice to your team's existing skills and how much customization you expect.
